question: Tell me about a time you were working under significant pressure or stress. How did you manage yourself and the work?

raiseTranscript.text: My first sprint had a tight deadline on a new API endpoint. I underestimated the edge cases and hit a blocker two days before launch.
I broke the remaining work into smaller tasks, flagged the risk in standup, and asked my mentor for a quick review on the tricky auth logic. I also blocked two hours each evening to avoid burnout.
We shipped on time. The endpoint passed load tests. I wrote a short retro note on estimation and shared it with the team.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you were working under significant pressure or stress. How did you manage yourself and the work?
Junior dev, first real deadline, API endpoint
Broke work down, asked mentor, protected evenings, shared retro note
"I flagged the risk in standup and asked for a quick review"
Follow-up: Asked how they handled the stress itself - said they used a checklist and talked to mentor instead of staying late every night
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Resilience for junior. Candidate owned an individual deliverable, sought help early, protected personal sustainability, and captured a learning artifact. Story shows they treated stress as a signal to adjust rather than push through alone. Biggest strength is the explicit ask for feedback and the retro note that turned personal pressure into team value.

lowerTranscript.text: We had a launch deadline and I just worked late every night until it was done.
Did you ask anyone for help?
Not really, I wanted to show I could handle it. I missed a couple of bugs that were found in prod.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Junior, launch deadline, solo late nights
No help sought, missed bugs in prod
"I wanted to show I could handle it"
Follow-up: Asked what changed after prod issues - candidate said they just tried to be more careful next time, no process change
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Candidate defaulted to heroics without surfacing risk or asking for input, resulting in production issues. No evidence of learning agility beyond "be more careful." The story stays at the level of individual endurance rather than adaptive ownership.

raiseTranscript.text: Our cross-team migration slipped and the other team was blocked. I was the on-call owner for the service.
How did you handle the pressure?

I created a shared rollback plan with the dependent team, set a daily 15-minute sync, and protected my own focus by delegating two on-call rotations. After we stabilized I wrote a post-mortem with clear owner changes.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Senior, cross-team migration slip, on-call owner
Shared rollback plan, daily sync, delegated rotations, post-mortem with owner changes
"I protected my own focus by delegating two on-call rotations"
Follow-up: Asked about personal stress management - said they blocked calendar time for exercise and used the post-mortem to close the loop instead of carrying the weight
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Shows influence across teams, deliberate delegation to sustain personal capacity, and a structural fix via post-mortem. Concrete actions (rollback plan, delegated rotations) produced measurable stability. Biggest strength is treating personal resilience as a team-leverage decision rather than solo endurance.

lowerTranscript.text: The migration was late so I just worked weekends until both teams were unblocked.
What changed for the next migration?
We added more buffer in the schedule but I still ended up owning most of the weekend work.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Senior, migration slip, worked weekends
No delegation or cross-team plan, repeated pattern next time
"I still ended up owning most of the weekend work"
Follow-up: Asked about learning - candidate described adding buffer but no process or ownership change
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Candidate absorbed the pressure personally without creating leverage or changing ownership patterns. Repeated weekend ownership shows limited learning agility. Story lacks cross-team influence or sustainable mechanisms.

raiseTranscript.text: Two engineers on my team burned out during a re-org crunch. I had to keep delivery moving while protecting the team.

I re-prioritized the roadmap with the director, moved two features to next quarter, and had 1:1s to redistribute work based on capacity. I also modeled leaving at 6pm and required the same of my leads.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Manager, re-org crunch, two engineers burning out
Roadmap re-prioritization, work redistribution, modeled boundaries
"I required the same of my leads"
Follow-up: Asked how they handled their own stress - said they used skip-levels for air cover and tracked team health metrics weekly
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Candidate made explicit trade-offs at the team level, redistributed load, and modeled sustainable behavior. Delivery continued while protecting people. Biggest strength is treating resilience as a leadership lever rather than personal endurance.

lowerTranscript.text: We lost two people to burnout so I pushed the remaining team harder to hit the date.
We hired replacements but kept the same delivery pressure for the next quarter.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Manager, re-org, two burnouts
Pushed harder, no boundary modeling, repeated pressure
"We hired replacements but kept the same delivery pressure"
Follow-up: Asked about team health signals - candidate had none beyond headcount
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Candidate responded to underperformance and burnout by increasing pressure instead of adjusting scope or support. No evidence of developing others or creating sustainable team norms. Pattern repeated in the following quarter.

raiseTranscript.text: A major product bet was at risk of missing market window after a platform outage. The whole org was stressed.
How did you lead through it?

I reset the company OKRs in a single all-hands, moved two strategic bets to later quarters, and created a 90-day recovery plan owned by two VPs. I also started a monthly leadership offsite focused on decision hygiene so the same overload wouldn't recur.

raiseNotes: Q: same
Exec, platform outage, org-level stress, product bet at risk
Reset OKRs, moved bets, 90-day plan with VP owners, monthly offsite on decision hygiene
"I created a monthly leadership offsite focused on decision hygiene"
Follow-up: Asked about personal sustainability - said they protected one unscheduled day per week and used the offsite to distribute strategic load
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Candidate made org-level trade-offs, distributed ownership, and installed a recurring mechanism to improve future decision quality. Actions addressed both immediate delivery and long-term org resilience. Biggest strength is converting acute stress into structural change.

lowerTranscript.text: We missed the window so I told the teams to work harder on the next release.
What org changes did you make?
We added headcount and tightened review processes but kept the same planning cadence.

lowerNotes: Q: same
Exec, missed market window
Told teams to work harder, added headcount, no planning change
"We added headcount and tightened review processes but kept the same planning cadence"
Follow-up: Asked about leadership sustainability - candidate described longer hours with no delegation of strategic decisions
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar. Candidate defaulted to intensity and headcount rather than strategic re-prioritization or process change. No evidence of long-term thinking or leverage through the organization. The response stays at heroic pressure instead of systemic judgment.
